title: Two pointers
summary: Two indexes moving through an array turn many O(n²) pair searches into one O(n) pass.

steps.title: Closing in from both ends
body: Find two numbers in a **sorted** array that add up to `target`. Checking every pair is `O(n²)`.

Instead put one pointer at each end. If their sum is too big, the right value is too big for *any* partner, so move `hi` left. Too small? Move `lo` right. Each step rules out one value for good, so it is `O(n)`.
Watch `lo` and `hi` walk towards each other until `4 + 6` hits 10.

steps.prompt: Same array, `target = 13`. What does it print?

steps.title: Read and write pointers
body: The other two-pointer shape has both pointers moving **forwards**: `read` scans every item, `write` marks where the next kept item goes. It edits an array **in place**.
To remove duplicates from a sorted array, keep an item only when it differs from the last kept one. Afterwards the first `write` slots hold the answer; whatever is beyond is leftover.
Watch `write` lag behind `read` every time a duplicate is skipped.

steps.prompt: Read/write pointers that move the non-zero values forward, then fill the rest with zeros. What does it print?
steps.explain: The non-zero values keep their order and slide to the front; the tail is zero-filled. One pass, no extra array.

steps.prompt: Complete the palindrome check: pointers start at both ends and move inwards.
steps.explain: When `i` meets or passes `j`, every pair has been compared. The middle character of an odd-length string needs no partner.

steps.prompt: Why does the pair-sum trick need the array to be **sorted**?
options: Moving a pointer must make the sum predictably bigger or smaller
Unsorted arrays have no last element
It does not: it works on any array
steps.explain: In a sorted array, moving `lo` right can only increase the sum and moving `hi` left can only decrease it. Without that, discarding a value could throw away the answer. For unsorted data use the HashSet approach instead.

steps.title: Palindrome, ignoring punctuation
prompt: Write `bool IsPalindrome(string s)` that ignores everything except letters and digits, and ignores case.
IsPalindrome("A man, a plan, a canal: Panama")   // true
Use two pointers on the original string and skip characters where `char.IsLetterOrDigit` is false. Do not build a cleaned copy and do not use `Reverse`.
template: Dojo.Eq("the Panama sentence", true, IsPalindrome("A man, a plan, a canal: Panama"));
Dojo.Eq("race a car", false, IsPalindrome("race a car"));
Dojo.Eq("Was it a car or a cat I saw?", true, IsPalindrome("Was it a car or a cat I saw?"));

forbid.message: Uses two pointers, not a cleaned or reversed copy

hints: Skip a non-alphanumeric character on either side with `continue` before comparing.

steps.title: Pairs and duplicates
prompt: - `int[] PairWithSum(int[] sorted, int target)`: indexes `{ lo, hi }` of two different positions whose values add to `target`, found by closing in from both ends; an empty array if none.
- `int RemoveDuplicates(int[] sorted)`: removes duplicates **in place** and returns how many distinct values now fill the front of the array. An empty array gives 0.
The tests use arrays of 500,000 items.
solution: if (sum == target) return new[] { lo, hi };
template: Dojo.Eq("no pair makes 13", new int[0], PairWithSum(new[] { 1, 3, 4, 6, 8, 11 }, 13));
Dojo.Eq("one item cannot pair with itself", new int[0], PairWithSum(new[] { 5 }, 10));
Dojo.Eq("equal values at two positions", new[] { 0, 1 }, PairWithSum(new[] { 5, 5 }, 10));
Dojo.Eq("the front holds the distinct values", new[] { 1, 2, 3, 4 }, dojoA[..dojoK]);
Dojo.Eq("RemoveDuplicates of an empty array", 0, RemoveDuplicates(new int[0]));
Dojo.Eq("500,000 items: pair found", new[] { 0, 499_999 }, PairWithSum(dojoBig, 249_999));
hints: `PairWithSum` is the first trace with `return new[] { lo, hi }` when the sum matches.
